name: Pinealon

card.summary: A Glu-Asp-Arg tripeptide from Khavinson's lab marketed for brain and anti-aging use; cell and rat data, only small Russian-language human reports.
card.note: Research peptide; not approved, and evidence is largely from one research network.

quick.overview:
Pinealon is a three-amino-acid peptide (glutamic acid, aspartic acid, arginine) developed in Russia as a brain-focused "bioregulator". It is promoted for neuroprotection and anti-aging.

Studies are mostly cell cultures and rats. A few Russian-language reports involve human groups, but details and independent replication are lacking.
quick.mechanism: Lab studies report that pinealon reduces reactive-oxygen-species build-up in cultured neurons and other cells and modulates signalling such as ERK 1/2 [1]. Labelled short peptides, including pinealon, were also reported to enter the cell nucleus and bind DNA in vitro [2].
quick.risks: No systematic safety data are available. It is not an approved medicine and is sold as a research peptide.

lead: Pinealon is a synthetic tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Arg (EDR) developed in Vladimir Khavinson's peptide bioregulator program. It is described as acting on the brain and nervous system, and it is discussed in nootropic and anti-aging circles.[5]

The appearance connection is indirect and is made mostly in anti-aging framing: peptide bioregulators are promoted for healthy-aging goals, and some people who pursue a younger, more rested look include them in broader longevity routines. No published study has examined pinealon's effects on skin, face or hair.

Published research consists of cell-culture studies and rat experiments, such as protection of rat offspring from prenatal hyperhomocysteinemia[3] and reduced oxidative stress in cultured cells,[1] along with Russian-language reports in human groups.[4][5] It is not an approved drug in the US or EU.

paras: In cerebellar granule cells, neutrophils and PC12 cells, pinealon was reported to restrict accumulation of reactive oxygen species in a dose-dependent way and to reduce necrotic cell death, alongside delayed ERK 1/2 activation [1]. In rats, giving pinealon to pregnant animals with experimental hyperhomocysteinemia was reported to improve offspring spatial learning and make cerebellar neurons more resistant to oxidative stress [3]. A study with fluorescence-labelled peptides, including pinealon, found they entered HeLa cells and nuclei and interacted with DNA oligonucleotides in vitro [2]. A Russian-language review compares pinealon with other peptide neuroprotectants such as semax [6].

A 2008 Russian-language study compared several short peptides (vilon, epitalon, vesugen and pinealon) in a model of hypobaric hypoxia and reported antihypoxic properties for all, with pinealon the most pronounced; the authors attributed this less to blocking the rise in reactive oxygen species than to stimulating other protective processes.[7] A 2014 report in old rats with acute hypoxia compared pinealon with Cortexin and concluded that pinealon was associated with increased neurogenesis markers and reduced neuroinflammatory reactions, measured through caspase-3 activity and cytokines (interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor).[8]

In vitro experiments with pinealon, vesugen, vilon and epitalon found that the peptides did not show direct antioxidant activity but could limit lipid peroxidation of human lipoproteins by modifying their structure, increased the stability of red-blood-cell membranes against osmotic hemolysis, and altered intracellular reactive-oxygen-species levels [12]. Further rat work from the same research network examined peptides given before carotid artery occlusion in old rats, measuring behavior and caspase-3 activity in the brain [13], and the effect of peptide geroprotectors on navigation learning and caspase-3 across ages [14].

A 2020 review in Molecules describes the EDR peptide as having neuroprotective properties in cell and animal studies: it is reported to activate expression of genes and synthesis of proteins that maintain neuronal activity, to reduce apoptosis, to preserve dendritic spines in cultured neurons from mouse models of Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease, and to activate antioxidant enzyme synthesis in rat cerebellar neurons.[9] The authors propose that the peptide enters cells and binds histone proteins or RNA, thereby altering activity of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, which matches the ERK 1/2 findings in cell studies.[1][9] The fluorescence-labelling study that showed entry into HeLa cell nuclei is the main direct evidence for cell penetration.[2] The sources do not report human pharmacokinetics.

Vladimir Khavinson (1946-2024) was a Russian gerontologist who directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology. Wikipedia credits him with developing peptide bioregulator therapy, with six peptide medicines approved in the USSR and Russia (mainly for military medicine, including Thymalin, Epithalamin and Cortexin) and many peptide food supplements, and notes his books Peptides and Ageing (2002) and Gerontological Aspects of Genome Peptide Regulation (2005) [11]. The same article is flagged as containing promotional content and relies largely on his own claims, including that the peptides lack toxic or adverse effects, without citing independent verification [11]. Pinealon is one of the short peptides in this family; the Wikipedia entry lists it among peptides of note without further detail [11].

Pinealon belongs to a family of short peptide bioregulators developed by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues, which also includes epitalon, vilon and vesugen and is the subject of a body of Russian gerontology literature, much of it in the journal Advances in Gerontology.[3][7][9] Pinealon (Glu-Asp-Arg) has been studied in nerve-cell models, hypoxia and aging.[1][3] A 2024 Russian-language review discusses short peptides as possible pharmacotherapy for Alzheimer's disease.[10]

Evidence in humans is limited to Russian-language reports. One describes peptide-based correction of neurotic disorders in professional truck drivers [4]; another examines synthetic peptides in elderly patients with chronic polymorbidity and organic brain syndrome [5]. A review describes clinical applications of neuroprotective peptides in elderly people [6]. No randomized, independently replicated trial of pinealon was found.

The truck-driver report compared 150 male lorry-drivers (mean age 43.3) with 150 male metal craftsmen (mean age 42.8) using clinical questionnaires to estimate psychoadaptive disorders before examining peptide correction [4]. A related Russian-language paper analyzed biological-age and adaptation parameters in locomotive-brigade workers [15]. A 2026 orthopaedic review lists pinealon alongside epithalon and delta sleep-inducing peptide as recovery-oriented peptides targeting circadian and mitochondrial regulators, while stating that clinical trials are lacking for the peptide class [16].
No systematic safety data in the sources. Pinealon is not an approved medicine in the US or EU.

chain: Short peptide proposed to enter cells and influence gene expression
Reported reduction of oxidative stress and cell death in lab models
Hoped-for support of brain function and healthy aging, with a possible rested, youthful presentation
angle.text: Users who include peptide bioregulators in anti-aging routines do so for brain and aging goals, with any visible benefit asserted rather than measured. Published work covers cultured cells, rats and a few Russian-language human reports; none examines facial appearance.
